title: Glossary
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-13 from the published page (posts/glossary/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the page, in its order; each section's lead paragraph and its table are one list-form unit with the table as evidence, and the callouts stand before p01 as the house format. Intent, acceptance criteria and role are copied unchanged from journal-spec.json; the journal spec gives a reference page no thesis, so the thesis here is the page's own and only orders its sections. A light pass for a lookup page: entries were checked for consistency against the ledger, the rulings and the chapters' settled definitions, not rewritten.

know: The book's terms in one or two plain sentences each, grouped by part, with standards and regulations and Kestrel & Pine names in their own tables, dated as of November 2026.
can_do: Look up a term met in a chapter, read it beside the terms it is confused with, and follow the link to the chapter that owns it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader finds the definition of a contrasted term pair used in the payment chapters and the chapter that owns it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what is the difference between authorization and capture, which chapters explain them, and why is 'capture on shipment' a promise with a deadline?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Authorization is the issuer approving and reserving the money; capture is the merchant taking it, often when the parcel ships. An authorization expires, so capture on shipment has a deadline. Owning chapters: commerce-payments and journey-consumer-order.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of chapter 25 finds the meaning of a term and of a Waypoint decision it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: chapter 25 uses 'idempotency' and 'W5'. What does each mean, and which chapters explain them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Idempotency: handling the same message twice has the same effect as handling it once (a second 'refund order #1072455' must not produce a second refund); journey-of-an-order and events-consistency-and-reconciliation. W5, integration standards: every integration has a named owner, a contract, idempotent handling of repeated messages and a reconciliation job; stock, orders and prices move by events, products by scheduled publication, finance by daily batch; integration-styles and meet-kestrel-and-pine.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader comparing GMV figures across chapters 41 and 46 learns why they may not match.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: chapter 41 discusses GMV-based pricing and chapter 46 reports Shopify's GMV. What is GMV, and why might the two figures be defined differently?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The value of orders passing through a platform, including what the platform does not keep; several vendors price on it. Definitions differ on refunds and fees: Shopify's filing calls it gross merchandise volume and counts it net of refunds, so read each source's definition.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of evidence or material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One definition per term with a link to the chapter that explains its use: why 'order' and 'in stock' mean different things in different systems; how to browse by part or use the alphabetical index; the opening section on evidence labels, take-away tiers, growth stages and failure patterns; separate tables for standards and regulations and for the fictional names; slash rows that define contrasted terms together. Material: the chapters' own definitions; Kestrel & Pine is fictional and legal entries defer to the cited source.

thesis.question: What does each commerce and architecture term used in the book mean?
thesis.claim: Each term the book uses has one plain definition that follows its owning chapter, set beside the terms it is confused with and linked to that chapter; standards are dated and defer to their source, and Kestrel & Pine's names are labelled fictional.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a reader can search the chapter or the web for a term, so a separate glossary only duplicates the chapters and drifts from them.
thesis.so_what: A reader who meets a term out of order gets the owning chapter's meaning in one place, with the neighbours it is confused with, and a writer or AI tool that finds a row and a chapter disagreeing has a defect to fix.
thesis.how_why: The definitions were harvested from each chapter's bold first-use definitions and definition tables and checked against the scenario ledger and the consistency rulings; slash rows set contrasted terms side by side, and every row links to its chapter.

supporting_claims.claim: A reader can find any term, alias or abbreviation by part or through the alphabetical index.
Each definition follows its owning chapter, sits beside its confusable neighbours and links to that chapter.
Standards, protocols and regulations carry their scope and a date and defer to the official source.
Kestrel & Pine's names are labelled fictional and agree with the scenario ledger.

role.contribution: Gives the book one vocabulary: each term's meaning, its confusable neighbors and the chapter that owns it, so a chapter can be read out of order.

flow.rationale: How to use the page comes first; the terms follow in the book's own order, from the reading conventions of the preface through Parts I to XI, so a reader who knows the chapter finds its section; the cross-cutting standards and the fictional names come after the parts they serve, and the alphabetical index closes the lookup for a reader who knows only the word.

hook.content: A storefront's 'order' can differ from an invoice or a warehouse shipment, and 'in stock' may mean physical stock, sellable stock or a stale copy.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader has met a term in a chapter, often read out of order, and the toolkit's cards closed by pointing to the definitions of the terms they use.
bridge.to_topic: Those differences in meaning change system behaviour and the conclusions drawn from reports, so each term needs one meaning and an owning chapter.

decision_log.decision: Converted spec.md to spec.json in a light pass for a lookup page: one spec paragraph per draft unit, each section's lead paragraph and table as one list-form unit with the table as evidence; the thesis is the page's own because the journal spec gives a reference page none. length.max_words is the published length plus 10%: 16,733 words as check_draft counts them (tables and Sources excluded; derived from the 16,993 after this pass less the 260 words it added), so 18,406; 19,095 by wc.
rejected: Specifying each table row as a paragraph
Carrying the old inventory-style success criteria over

decision_log.decision: Auto-resolved by the author's standing instruction of 2026-11-12: the GMV open question is settled by consistency ruling 20 (in this book GMV is before refunds and returns; a company's reported GMV follows its own definition); the row now says so and keeps Shopify's net-of-refunds definition as the example.
rejected: Leaving the row saying only that definitions differ

decision_log.decision: Auto-resolved by the author's standing instruction of 2026-11-12: the SKU open question is settled by consistency ruling 21 (the glossary follows chapter 06; 'a SKU' for the variant is accepted shorthand); the row already does both.
rejected: Changing the row to the ledger's wording

decision_log.decision: Consistency fixes to book-wide vocabulary and the ledger, entries otherwise unchanged: 'Commerce platform' row now gives chapter 1's meaning (the whole set of systems that make and keep promises) and chapter 5's market sense, named the shop platform; 'The platform' row renamed 'The shop platform' with 41 apps in January 2027 and 34 by July 2027 (ruling 10); 'System' takes chapter 1's definition; added 'Status line' (chapter 1's definition) and 'single writer' to the copy / writer row (chapter 4's ownership test); system of record and ATP aligned with chapters 4 and 10; handoff adds chapter 1's acceptance rule; stock sync chain says 'up to two hours' with no hop intervals; 'commerce platform' and 'SaaS platform' meaning the hosted product changed to 'shop platform' in two rows; a first sentence saying what the page is for and how to use it added to p01; index entries added for the new and renamed rows.

After draft-check round 1 (REVISE), cheap fixes applied without a second round: the opening paragraph states its purpose once with the 'order' / 'in stock' examples as the reason and now names the preface, slash rows, standards table and fictional names (AC-4); the preface is described the same way in How to Use and its own paragraph; Part V's lead is a sentence that no longer calls the back office an outside party; Duiven and Waypoint W6 link to the Kestrel & Pine section; the Build / buy / assemble row maps the four shapes onto the three verbs (chapter 41's table); the standards column 'Short name' renamed 'Name'; the Kestrel lead says the scenario runs into 2028; a blank line and a one-sentence lead-in (part of p19's list unit) added before the index; fifteen 'X' index entries that duplicated 'The X' at the same anchor removed; the conclusion gains the synthesis, callback and so-what sentence. The page was not re-checked after these edits.
rejected: A second draft-check round (the brief allows one)
Linking index entries to rows (needs row anchors from the generator)

decision_log.decision: Mirrored the sibling glossaries: grouped by part, evidence labels and failure patterns first, fictional names last, index generated from the tables by _research/glossary-tools/assemble.py from rows.py.

Replaced the sibling's market-register table with a 'Standards, Protocols and Regulations' table (term, scope, short name, meaning, chapter), because this book's external vocabulary is EU law, national e-invoicing and fiscal rules, US rules and global standards.
Definitions harvested from each chapter's bold first-use definitions and definition tables, then trimmed by dropping minor mechanisms and failure-handling cases; slash rows hold contrasted terms.
WHY IT MATTERS callout omitted, following the author's decision to drop it from every page.

Auto-resolved by the author's instruction of 2026-11-13: the generator is kept, and the 2026-11-12/13 hand edits of index.md (intro and How to Use paragraphs, section intros, revised and added rows, the 'Name' column header, the index lead sentence, the closing paragraph, icon and logo) are carried into _research/glossary-tools/rows.py, head.md, tail.md and assemble.py; rerunning assemble.py reproduces the page except that two index links under C ('Commerce platform', 'Commerce platform / shop platform') come out in alphabetical order, so the page was left as it is. Rerun the generator in each review cycle and edit rows.py, not index.md; rejected: retiring the generator and maintaining the page by hand.
